fullText:
For around 15 hours, immigration detention officers kept Raúl Suárez Herrero confined in a cage slightly larger than a phone booth, where he feared snakes and endured mosquitoes in the middle of Florida swampland, the former detainee alleged.

Suárez, 59, told José Díaz-Balart in an interview for Noticias Telemundo’s “Ahora 360” that he was forced into the cage, measuring 7 feet, 9 inches high and 4 feet, 3 inches square, for praying out loud for an ill young man at “Alligator Alcatraz,” an ICE detention site.

“I feel like I was in hell,” Suárez later told NBC News in a phone interview from Mexico, where he was deported.

Suárez spoke days after a Department of Homeland Security watchdog confirmed the use of the phone booth-sized cages at the now-shuttered Florida detention camp in a Sept. 11 report.

“The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” the report said.

The DHS Office of Inspector General report documented its inspectors’ findings during an unannounced January visit to the Ochopee, Florida, site.

In December, Amnesty International issued its own report on conditions at the detention site based on interviews with detainees and its own tour of the facility. The organization detailed the use of the small cages and said it amounted to torture.

The facility staff told inspectors that the cages were “calming areas” where immigrants could de-escalate and have time alone and that no one spent more than two hours inside them.

But Suárez told Noticias Telemundo that “they took me there and I spent more than 15 hours inside in that little hole,” referring to the small cage. He said he was forced in around 1 p.m. and taken out at about 5 a.m. “when morning was breaking.” According to Suárez, the cage was in a recreation area where detainees took exercise time. Suárez said he couldn’t stretch out on the cage floor and got little sleep for fear of what might slither into the cage.

“I had to be careful because on the ground there were snakes and you don’t see them. You can’t fall asleep because they can come into the cage,” Suárez said in a video interview.

DHS did not directly address Suárez’s allegations or case in response to questions from NBC News. But a spokesperson rejected “claims that there were ‘inhumane’ conditions” at the immigrant detention center. Those claims are “categorically false” and any allegations of excessive use of force are “FALSE,” the spokesperson said in an email.

“No detainees were being beaten or abused,” the DHS spokesperson said. DHS provides long-standing medical, dental and mental health services, three meals a day that are evaluated by certified dietitians, clean water, clothing, bedding and hygiene products and access to phones to talk with family and lawyers, the spokesperson stated.

Alligator Alcatraz’s standards were consistent with those under other administrations, the spokesperson also said. Further questions were referred to the state of Florida, “as this facility was managed by the State of Florida through the Division of Emergency Management.”

The facility in the heart of the Everglades was built by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis as part of the state’s push to support President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

Alex Lafranconi, a spokesman for DeSantis, has dismissed criticism of the small cages. Lafranconi has described the small cages as a confinement area for “violent criminal aliens who have proven they cannot remain peaceful,” and said “we’d make them smaller, if we could.”

Although DHS said the inspector general “indicated” all recommendations have been administratively closed, the OIG said in its report that the administration did not address its 10 recommendations, including that it “discontinue the use of the small metal enclosures to hold detainees for any reason or amount of time.”

The OIG also said that at the time of the inspection, all the detainees were ICE detainees and there was evidence that ICE had some degree of oversight authority and engagement at the facility.

Originally from Cuba and in the U.S. since he was 12, Suárez was detained by ICE in July 2025 during an ICE check-in.

Before it was recently ordered closed, Alligator Alcatraz had been denounced by multiple detainees and legal and immigrant advocates for its conditions.

The detention facility’s records state the average time people were placed in the smaller cages with metal fencing was 59 minutes and 27 seconds, according to the OIG report. But the OIG said it could not confirm or refute ICE officials’ assertions regarding use of the enclosures or detainees’ allegations they had been denied food or other abuses.

The small cages at the facility were supposed to be a “safe and secure place” where people could “reflect on their behavior choices, manage their emotions, reduce stress, and practice self-directed behavior,” according to the detention camp’s policies, the report stated.

According to detention center records cited by the OIG, 79 people were held in the small cages during the period of July 17, 2025, to Jan. 18, and none were held more than two hours. Detainees in the small cage “may leave at any time by detainee request or per staff directive,” according to the report.

But Suárez was adamant that his confinement was not voluntary and lasted far more than two hours.

“Everybody lied” about the small cages, Suárez said, disputing that he could have gotten out or requested to be let out.

He said he was forced into the cage after praying out loud for a man who had an epileptic seizure as they were waiting to get registered at the detention camp.

Help for the man was taking “too long,” according to Suárez. That’s when he said he started praying aloud, as he used to do at the evangelical church he attended before his arrest.

“I asked God for the young man’s life,” he said.

Suárez alleged two guards then forced him to stand up, asked where he was from and then grabbed him and dragged him “all the way back to where that little cell was.” He said he was kicked in the leg so hard he thought they broke it. “My leg was so big and black.”

“They just dropped me over there and locked the doors,” he said. He said he got no medical treatment for his leg or a medical evaluation after the confinement.

Suárez said his experience has left him psychologically “shattered.”

Suárez was removed to Mexico in February after more than four decades of living in the United States. He was detained on July 16, 2025, when he went to an immigration check-in.

Suárez had been ordered removed from the U.S. in 2000 after serving a prison sentence stemming from a plea agreement on a drug charge. Because Cuba was not accepting U.S. deportees then, Suárez was released and told to check in with ICE annually, a court document states. Cuba has allowed few of its citizens to return after U.S. deportation.

An attorney attempted to get Suárez released from detention. The federal judge had given DHS until late January to remove him or release him, but the judge then extended the government’s time for two weeks. On the deadline date, Feb. 11, DHS deported Suárez to Mexico and the judge closed the case.

“Forty-seven years. They took me to the U.S. as a 12-year-old, when I was a child,” Suárez said. “I was raised my whole life there [in the U.S.]. I’m bilingual and everything. I went to school there and everything. And everything happened from one moment to the next. I still can’t absorb what happened.”

Suárez said he had been a truck driver since he was 17 and had built his own truck driving business with his brother, an American citizen, who died in 2021 from Covid. His father had died in Cuba when he was 3 and his mother, who became a U.S. citizen, died about a decade ago.

When immigration laws were toughened in 1996, making legal residents deportable for certain crimes, he could no longer seek U.S. citizenship, he said.

His mother had urged him to get citizenship, but he didn’t do it, he said.

“I was pretty young. When you are pretty young, you don’t listen to anybody,” he said. He had no other encounters with law enforcement, he said. He said he’d been living a normal life, preparing to buy a house and had a girlfriend.

“Life is changed. I don’t know what is going to happen here in Mexico.”

title: Hundreds of thousands rally in Iran in biggest anti-U.S. display since war began
description:
— Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied Friday in a government-organized show of defiance after months of war, pledging their readiness to take up arms in the biggest such demonstration since the United States and Israel attacked in February.
Iran's government has sought to rally the people and stress national unity, even as the economy worsens under a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and new U.S.
fullText:
CAIRO (AP) — Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied Friday in a government-organized show of defiance after months of war, pledging their readiness to take up arms in the biggest such demonstration since the United States and Israel attacked in February.

Iran's government has sought to rally the people and stress national unity, even as the economy worsens under a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and new U.S. sanctions. On Friday, it claimed another attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway it has sought to control since the start of the war.

Estimates varied of the number of people volunteering to receive limited military training and defend the country in an effort described as "Janfaday-e Iran," or the "ones who sacrifice their lives for Iran." They marched through downtown Tehran in combat uniform, carrying flags, as onlookers cheered.

For days, state media have encouraged Iranians to join the campaign, saying training with assault rifles would begin soon. The volunteers would be an additional layer of security to the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard and the Basij militia, which has played a key role in quashing anti-government protests.

Tehran's Guard chief, Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, told the state broadcaster that over 600,000 people had registered to participate, with over 1 million expected to take part in the training. On Friday morning, the broadcaster estimated over 300,000 people were on the streets.

The new head of the Basij, Hossein Taeb, declared in a speech as the rally began that the volunteers will be ready for "full-fledged defense" and similar rallies will take place in other cities soon.

The new trainees will make a "nightmare" for Iran's enemies, Taeb added, as President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders and other senior officials watched the march.

Some participants trampled flags of the U.S. and Israel. Others chanted "Death to America" and "Death to Israel."

"I am here to tell (U.S. President Donald) Trump that we Iranians have no fear about his threats against our homeland," said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her toddler and husband. "No one in history could invade Iran and remain there."

The rally was also a chance for Iran to show off military hardware. Anti-aircraft batteries were on display, while female Guard members in black headscarves sat with truck-mounted machine guns.

The Guard displayed drones that have been used against ships in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran's attacks and threats have severely affected the Gulf region's shipments of oil and natural gas to the rest of the world.

Iran said it had attacked a Togo-flagged oil tanker, the Trend, for what it called an "illegal attempt" to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the state broadcaster reported. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center said a tanker was hit by a projectile, sparking a fire on board that was extinguished.

The UKMTO in a separate update said ship transits facilitated by the U.S. military off Oman have averaged 24 a day over the past week but overall traffic remains about 90% lower than before the war.

Friday's events also suggested that hard-liners like Taeb among Iran's leadership will be more prepared to suppress any future demonstration against the theocracy.

In January, shortly before the war, Iran saw some of its largest nationwide protests in history, which began over the struggling economy and turned to wider grievances. Activists have said a crackdown killed over 7,000 people and saw tens of thousands detained.

In May, government officials said more than 30 million people in Iran — which has a total population of some 90 million — had volunteered via an online form or at public gatherings to lay down their lives for the theocracy. The Associated Press could not independently confirm that.

Karimi reported from Tehran, Iran, and Anna from Jerusalem.

fullText:
President Donald Trump has lashed out at leakers in his own administration after a series of behind-the-scenes reports on the Iran war.

As the conflict Trump claimed would be over in six weeks drags into its seventh month, insiders have repeatedly claimed the president was warned against taking action by his own advisors.

“Keep on leaking you dirty dogs! When we find you, you will pay a big price!!!” declared on his Truth Social Thursday night.

The president was responding to an editorial in The Washington Post addressing the war in Iran and a Wall Street Journal report last month revealing that his then-director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, advised him against launching Operation Epic Fury on February 28.

Click here for the latest on the war.

Marc Thiessen’s piece condemned the “self-serving leaks” and said they had ultimately only served to demonstrate “what a courageous decision Trump made” when choosing to stop the nuclear threat posed by Tehran while “surrounded by naysayers” and “doves.”

The journalist argued the “most tragic mistake that world leaders made over the past century was the failure to take the words of the monsters of history seriously” – naming Vladimir Lenin, Adolf Hitler and Osama Bin Laden. He claimed Trump had bucked the trend and made “the bravest foreign policy decision any president has done in my lifetime.”

“Even if it hurts him politically in November, he will be rewarded by history,” Thiessen concluded.

The president hailed his article as “very interesting” and “a must read,” which counts as rare praise for a newspaper he has regularly derided and which he attempted to sue for defamation in 2023, only for the $3.8 billion lawsuit to be thrown out in July.

The war has proved domestically unpopular for Trump just as the country heads to the midterms, with Reuters / Ipsos polling last month suggesting just 31 percent of Americans support the conflict.

Previous reports have suggested Trump was persuaded to unleash war on Iran by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu despite skepticism from his inner circle.

Vice President JD Vance was the most vocal in his opposition, according to a New York Times report in April, with CIA Director Jim Ratcliffe, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Gen. Dan Caine said to have claimed Netanyahu “oversold” the president.

Since then, the cost of the war has spiralled to an estimated $33 billion, sent gas prices soaring and all but closed the key shipping route the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump previously lashed out at leakers in August after it was reported he had had an argument with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at Camp David over a reported shortfall on U.S. missile stockpiles as a result of the war.

“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down,” the president fumed. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!”

Similarly, he has previously warned his enemies they will “pay a big price,” doing so in July when ranting about the “vandals” and “sleazebags” he insisted had sabotaged his restoration of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

title: AI Is a Kitchen-Table Issue
description: Chris...
fullText:
And with the Trump administration encouraging unregulated growth in the industry, Democrats need to start acting like it.

The Republican Party sports a glaring weakness in the pitched battle over regulating the rapidly multiplying abuses of AI, and its name is Donald John Trump. The president sought to dismiss the growing furor about the multitude of threats the unregulated new technology poses to our basic quality of life by proclaiming on Truth Social that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”

But while the MAGAfied GOP is ambling cluelessly into yet another political firestorm, the Democratic Party is lapsing once more into its resting-shrug posture. Yes, there are serious hazards associated with the blind lunge into all things AI—up to and including species extinction—party elders and strategists concede, but it’s important not to get carried away on the tide of public outrage. So, as Trump fulminated and flattered himself, House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries announced the appointment of a new AI policy panel made up mostly of flacks and shills for the industry. Because whenever the leaders of an economic sector let it slip that they may well be programming the imminent demise of humanity, the first thing you do is grant them the authority to make up their own rules of oversight.

Jeffries’s gambit was, alas, a continuation of the party’s dilatory-to-negligent approach to all things AI. During the 119th Congress, Democratic lawmakers have mostly marshaled themselves behind vague and airy bids to draft regulation of the industry through bipartisan task forces stressing broad alignment on the issue, an approach that has yielded much the same results the most such initiatives do. “Congressional leaders have let bipartisan working groups fall apart, dragging out progress on issues lawmakers from both parties say they could get a meaningful majority behind,” NOTUS reporter Samuel Larreal wrote late last year. Even though some 400 pending bills in 2025 had addressed the many threats poised by untrammeled AI development, none gained traction; indeed, the most dogged GOP-driven campaign was to deregulate the industry further, via language in both the tax-and-spending and defense authorization bills that would have preempted state and local governments from curbing the growth of AI data centers and applications in their midst.

This lost opportunity stands out in high relief now, as Democratic leaders try to launch belated new bids to rein in the excesses of the AI sector before Congress adjourns for the midterms—and as a new cohort of Democratic-aligned PACs push for a more robust Democratic response to the uprising against it. (Lest you think this latter development signals any sort of fundamental change in establishment thinking, the party’s lead consultants and strategists are still urging candidates to avoid angering AI moguls in the homestretch of the midterms, lest they unleash their well-funded PACs on rebellious Democratic candidates in tight races.) The specter of yet more legislative hand-waving in the face of a mounting oligarchic assault on the basic quality of life in thousands of American communities is especially hard to take, the industry’s predations fall into the category that Democrats continually insist is the topic of their laser-focused attention: the frantic, unsupervised buildout of AI capacity is the essence of a kitchen-table issue.

Leaving aside the speculative forecasts of the technology’s potential role in snuffing out humanity, AI is already acting as a fearsome accelerant on the growth of inequality in the United States. It’s not hard to see why: The AI investment bubble, which has been set aloft on a series of circular financing schemes benefiting the tech power elite, has created an upward surge in the distribution of wealth that makes the run-up to the 2008 Great Recession look like the Paris Commune. JPMorgan estimates that just 30 AI stocks have added $5.2 trillion in paper wealth to US households—with most of that return confined to the top 10 percent of investors. Indeed, the bubble has accounted for an additional $180 billion in spending from these rarefied households, the Morgan analysts found, as most middle- and working-class households fend off higher energy and healthcare costs while sinking ever deeper into debt. While reports claim that AI investment now accounts for 40 percent or more of the country’s GDP growth, the subset of economic actors actually benefiting from the bubble is vanishingly small—and are mostly confined to the charmed circle of the tech oligarchy. Fully 80 percent of the enterprise revenues claimed by Anthropic and OpenAI, writes industry critic Ed Zitron, “are dependent on what are likely hundreds of customers spending outsized amounts of money on AI tokens, with an indeterminately-large chunk of them being AI startups that can only do so as long as venture capital supports them.”

And just like the mid-aughts housing bubble, the AI investment stampede is creating acute conditions of inequality on the ground—in towns, school districts, and workplaces. To begin with, there’s the push to cram data centers into virtually any low-tax, underregulated jurisdiction that can be cajoled into housing them. These engines of water scarcity, electricity-bill spikes, and noise pollution are the prime mover behind the populist uprising against AI in red and blue states alike, with hapless elected officials and candidates awkwardly vying to keep up. Polling shows that 75 percent of Americans oppose the erection of data centers in their communities, with just 15 percent supporting them.

The runaway appropriation of resources, land, and capital by the AI sector is, in other words, the mother of all kitchen-table issues—and by extension, shopfloor, roadway, and classroom ones, as our data lords seek to annex virtually every facet of our productive and civic life into their feverishly privating hands. Public education, long held to be the magic elixir of upward social mobility in the US economy, is rapidly becoming a bot playground, with predictably harmful fallout for students’ cognitive development while fomenting an epidemic of cheating and fraud. While early forecasts of an AI job apocalypse appear overblown, the technology’s role in promulgating surveillance-state protocols on the job decidedly is not.

So why is it that Democrats remain on their back heels in the midst of the AI uprising? One key explanation is that they benefit from the same Big Tech donations that have juiced Republican campaign coffers. Hakeem Jeffries has opposed a moratorium on data-center construction, and has detailed industry mouthpieces like California Representative Zoe Lofgren to draw up the Democratic caucus’s AI policy. This disconnect between the party’s leadership caste and the specter of a grassroots revolt in an election cycle has become so pronounced that former president Barack Obama has intervened. “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous,” Obama told Jeffries at a New York City donors’ event last week. Looking ahead to the 2028 presidential cycle, he cautioned that Democratic candidates must have a “very clear plan” to address the imminent risks posed by the technology. “I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety. Here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this.’”

Obama, a longtime confrere of Big Tech titans, explained that he regards himself as neither a “doomer” or “accelerationist” on the AI front—but his political advice recalls the same lurch into populist rhetoric that attended his 2012 reelection campaign, when he had the great good fortune of drawing private capital baron Mitt Romney as his opposing candidate. As was the case then, Democrats have a terminally out-of-touch apostle of the investment class symbolizing the rush to adopt AI at all costs: President Donald Trump, who has fruitlessly sought to tamp down the rebellion against data centers in the house of MAGA. At the outset of his second term, Trump issued an executive order dismantling the Biden White House’s body of safety protocols governing the industry, while his Environmental Protection Agency and Justice Department have dedicated themselves to speeding along the unregulated rollout of data centers.

Trump is also, as a majority of polled respondents now acknowledge, staggeringly corrupt, so it shouldn’t be a heavy lift for Democrats to make the case that his desperate shilling for data centers—like his self-interested reversal on crypto and a fetid run of stock trades outpacing the investment calls of every member of Congress during his second term—serves to line his pockets and shower more pelf on his inner circle of cronies. Just for starters, Donald Trump Jr.’s venture-capital fund 1789 Capital has realized returns of more than 200 percent as of the end of this June, with many of the gains coming from aggressive AI investments.

The attack ads pretty much write themselves: Donald Trump is despoiling your communities, spiking your utility bills, rationing your water, and leaving your kids at the mercy of robots so he can clean up even more on the AI bubble. All we need now is a political party with the backbone to make them credible.

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel

title: UConn men's basketball begin official practices next week, kicking off a busy preseason
description: Huskies can start practices on Monday, six weeks prior to season opener on Nov. 2.
fullText:
The UConn men's basketball team's quest for a seventh national championship, a third in five seasons, and a fourth trip to the Final Four over that same span begins with their first official practice on Monday.

Unless Dan Hurley decides to push it back to Tuesday.

Point is, the Huskies can officially begin practices on Monday, six weeks prior to their season-opener on Nov. 2 against Gardner-Webb in either Hartford or Storrs (more on that later). Up until now, over the summer and since returning to campus prior to Labor Day, UConn was limited to eight hours a week of workouts, with no more than four hours per week on the court.

On Monday (or possibly Tuesday, depending on Hurley's discretion) that gets bumped up to 20 hours per week for the rest of the season.

It will be a busier (and earlier) preseason for the Huskies. The days of First Night celebrations are long gone, replaced by exhibition games (i.e., money-makers) against high-level opponents. And teams can now have three preseason exhibitions, up from two. UConn's first will be Oct. 13 against Syracuse at Mohegan Sun Arena, followed by at Michigan State on Oct. 20 in East Lansing, Mich., then against Purdue (either in Hartford or Storrs) on Oct. 27.

Before that, there's Big East Media Day on Oct. 1 at the Marriott Marquis in Manhattan. This will be the first time in more than a decade that the annual gathering of coaches and key players for the upcoming season won't be held at Madison Square Garden. Seems Harry Styles has a residency at MSG in October, and coupled with the Knicks and Rangers' schedules, sneaking in a media day at the World's Most Famous Arena proved too tricky a task.

Media day is also much earlier than normal this year, likely a preview of the future. Many other leagues have held and are holding their respective men's and women's basketball media days in early October, in no small part due to the proliferation of more, high-level exhibition games that start in early/mid-October. (And, in this case, Harry Styles' MSG residency).

There will be other events cropping up over the next six weeks, including Hurley's annual visit to the Middlesex County Chamber of Commerce member breakfast on Oct. 5. And, of course, there will continue to be official visits from top-notch recruits over the next month, including Jordan Page, the No. 11 overall prospect in the Class of 2027, per 247Sports.com's composite rankings, this weekend.

Finally, on Nov. 2, the games start to count. Both the UConn men and women open their season that day, and it was announced on Thursday that the UConn women's season-opener against Cornell will be at Hartford's PeoplesBank Arena. That means the UConn men's opener against Gardner-Webb will be at Gampel Pavilion, right?

Not necessarily. Seems there could be some sort of split doubleheader in the works at Hartford, not unlike last Columbus Day's exhibition doubleheader at Mohegan Sun against the Huskies' counterparts from Boston College. That won't be known for sure until UConn releases its venue sites and tip-off times for all home games, likely early next week.

title: Giants news: Cornerbacks hurting, Matt Nagy praises Jaxson Dart, more
description: New York Giants headlines for Friday.
fullText:
Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as the Giants get set for their Monday night game against the Los Angeles Rams.

Giants fans who were trepidatious about the additions of Matt Nagy and Greg Roman as offensive architects have to feel great about what they saw in Week 1. The Giants were the league's second-best offense during the opening week of the season by EPA per play, trailing only the Bears. Their 58% success rate was second behind the Jaguars. The only reason they didn't score more points was time; the Giants used more time per play than anybody else in the league and had only seven possessions in their 28-20 victory over Dallas.

As a passer, Dart didn't have a huge game working from under center, going 5-of-7 for 39 yards with a 2-yard touchdown pass to Isaiah Likely. In all, though, the Giants looked comfortable majoring under center, something they ran only 20% of the time while Dart was on the field a year ago. It's a positive sign for their offensive progress, although the Rams might offer a more imposing defense to Dart this week on "Monday Night Football."

Jaxson Dart & the Giants are for real….completely different offense with Isaiah Likey out there. pic.twitter.com/W4IphKF45K

The scene was common on the practice fields with the New York Giants all summer.

Starting in West Virginia and continuing in New Jersey, seemingly every day of training camp, Jaxson Dart and Isaiah Likely would be standing together talking football. They would chat up different route concepts, the rules to follow for offscript plays and, above all else, gain comfort in the trust between them.

Dart said Donald's "real impact on the game" — beyond his 111 sacks, eight first-team All-Pro selections and three Defensive Player of the Year awards — stems from how offenses must scheme around him.

"For the longest time that I can remember, he's one of the most dominant players that I've watched," Dart said. "So getting the chance to go out there and compete against him, it's going to be really cool, just to be on the same field as him. He's a great player, and I've heard that he's kept himself in really good shape. So it's going to be a great competition. There's countless clips of putting three offensive linemen on him and [Donald] still being able to make a play. So he's an unbelievable player and has had an unbelievable career."

Players always say they need to clean up whatever mistakes they made in one game before they hit the field for the next game. Dru Phillips is in that mode this week.

The third-year cornerback was called for three pass interference penalties in the season-opening 28-20 victory over the Cowboys.

Harbaugh's resume gave him instant credibility throughout the organization and in the locker room. But the buy-in could fade if the results don't follow the hard work. That's why Sunday's impressive start has made the Giants even stronger believers in Harbaugh's methods.

"I don't think anyone would shy away from saying it was the hardest training camp of their career," 10th-year veteran right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor said. "I've been around Harbs (in Baltimore), and this was a physical-ass training camp. Now you know why you run that many plays in practice, why you hit as much, why you do those practices, why you lift as much as we do, how hard we work because you go out there on Sunday and, you really beat a team up like that."

[Extremely John Harbaugh voice] The New York GIANTS are legit contenders. I'll admit it! I was overconfident that the Giants would stumble out of the gate. I (like an idiot) was high on the Cowboys offense and expected Dallas to experience some positive defensive regression after letting Matt Eberflus loose and replacing him at DC with football nerd icon Christian Parker. But Harbaugh's new disgusting brothers in the booth— offensive coordinator Matt Nagy and assistant Greg Roman —took out a paddle and spanked the silver off the Cowboys' pants for all to see.

I'm a believer in the tone the Giants want to set and Skattebo's ability to set it, but I am not buying fully in just yet. The only defense worse than Big Blue's in Week 1 (again, by EPA per drive) was Parker's disasterclass. Let's see Harbaugh and his guys throw the same haymakers against the Rams with Sean McVay and Co. in a must-win spot coming off their Melbourne embarrassment.

Mission 34's motto, "A New Type of Tough," was painted on Jones' cleats. The five-word slogan is aimed at those who may be struggling with their mental health, especially athletes, with the goal of helping them realize that toughness isn't defined by a lack of vulnerability, the Bonners said. They believe, along with Jones, that there is strength — and life — in speaking up. Last November wasn't the first time Jones teamed up with Mission 34, having represented the organization during his New York Giants days, and it won't be his last. Jones considers it a worthy cause, and he's keenly aware of the NFL spotlight he wields.

title: Connecticut high school football teams will travel 6,138 miles in Alliance Week
description: Connecticut's Alliance Week will include 29 teams traveling at least 100 miles round trip.
fullText:
Driving in Connecticut is fun, fun, fun.

That's triple the fun and a whole bunch of sarcasm for those in the know.

It's a small state, but it features a cobweb of arteries merging into each other at choke points, making navigation difficult.

For the state's high school football teams, road trips near and far are a way of life. But add in traffic - and the state has plenty of that - the copious construction, especially around I-91 in Meriden, and the fact that buses are generally prohibited from traveling on Route 15, and the aggravation factor can skyrocket.

And, if a distance is far enough, an away team is sometimes left with few, if any, fans in the stands.

This week is Alliance Week, filled with interconference games courtesy of the Connecticut High School Football Alliance, which now includes all eight of the state's conferences. Alliance games create matchups between teams that normally would not face each other unless they met in a tournament setting.

That leads to two words: Road trip!

So to "celebrate," we've broken out some numbers travel-wise for this week's games, during which teams will log 6,138 miles of travel this weekend, with several closing in on 200 miles round trip.

For comparison, 6,138 miles is approximately ...

10,802,880 yards (we are talking football here, after all)

90,024 football fields, including end zones

approximate laps around a football field (more or less depending on how coaches feel after practice)

approximate number of baseball fields, assuming 360 feet to dead center

24.7% of the Earth's circumference

56 East-West trips (110 miles) across Connecticut

8 trips across Texas (Connecticut isn't very big, is it?)

Of the 66 road teams crisscrossing the state, 29 will log at least 100 miles round trip, topped by Darien's trip to Norwich Free Academy, which is 95 miles one-way and a 190-mile round trip. That game kicks off Friday at 6:30 p.m., and a victory and maybe some pizza would likely make that return trip more palatable.

Here's a breakdown of the longest distances with round-trip mileage:

190: Darien at Norwich Free Academy, Friday, 6:30 p.m.

184: Waterford at New Fairfield, Saturday, noon

180: Torrington at Fitch, Friday, 6:30 p.m.

176: Woodland at Killingly, Friday, 6:30 p.m.

168: McMahon at Manchester, Friday, 6 p.m.

As for the rest, traveling 100 or more miles:

On the short end, six teams will travel fewer than 40 miles round trip, a virtual stone's throw if your arm is strong enough. The shortest trip of 12 miles, 24 miles round trip, belongs to Rocky Hill, which faces Cheney Tech/Windham Tech at Cheney Tech on Friday at 6:30 p.m.

New London's trip to E.O. Smith on Friday at 6 p.m. is 37 miles each way. It's the same distance no matter the vehicle but likely faster by motorcycle.

As far as long road trips go, No. 10-ranked Fairfield Prep went 162 miles one-way over three states for its game at Scranton Prep (Pa.) in Week 1. The Jesuits actually departed a day early, on Thursday, and stayed overnight while preparing for their game.

In comparison, this week's road trip is an 18-mile jaunt down I-95 for Fairfield Prep, which plays at No. 1 New Canaan on Friday at 7 p.m.

Back to the Blue Wave, Darien has actually made the 95-mile trip to NFA recently, in 2021, when it defeated the Wildcats 49-7 in another Alliance game.

Darien will likely spend the majority of the ride on I-95 (there's that fun part again) before taking I-395 north to Norwich.

For Waterford and Torrington, whose trips also top 90 miles one way, the travel is a bit more involved and could hit several major roadways.

At the end of the day, road trips are what teams make of them. They can be unifying, challenging, tiring, perhaps even all three.

But they're almost always memorable, and with the playoff vibe that abounds around Alliance games, the weekend should be one to remember.

title: Broncos players react to ugly loss against Kansas City
description: Bo Nix, Pat Surtain II and Courtland Sutton reflected on Denver’s tough loss and what the Broncos must do going forward.
fullText:
It's not a matter of if, but when. For the Denver Broncos, it just happens to come a little earlier than some (most) would have liked. But how the Broncos respond to the beatdown at the hands of the Kansas City Chiefs this Sunday will reveal what kind of makeup they have.

To add to the motivation, Denver faces the Jacksonville Jaguars, a team that thoroughly whipped it 34-20 a season ago.

The good news is the Broncos have been in this position before under Sean Payton, going 4-8 in and struggling in September games heading into Sunday.

Week 2 work. 💪 pic.twitter.com/f0wwVGVDI2

"I learned a long time ago, you never play as bad as you think and you never play as good as you think," Broncos quarterback Bo Nix said to the media on Thursday. "So for us, it was the case of we didn't play as bad as what we thought. We just there at the end of the game, we didn't make third-down conversions. We felt like it was 7-7, 14-7, and 21-7 for a long time in the game. So it was reachable, and we were in it for a while.

"We just didn't help ourselves by any means. You watch the film, and there are a couple good things and then all of a sudden we're back because of a penalty or something. You just can't win in this league like that. So, overall, we're not going to press the panic button, and we're not freaking out. We're not starting from scratch or anything. We're still in a good spot, and we just didn't play great by any means, and we've got to play better."

The first step to correcting what went wrong against the Chiefs is the work at practice this week. As Nix said after the game on Monday, it was a "nasty wake-up call."

After that, it's about the players doing their job, doing the little things, and executing.

"We all know we are a very talented team, no question about it," Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain II said to the media. "That's why I feel like everybody has us on the high horse and stuff like that. That comes with a certain privilege. But if you don't show up each and every week, you're going to get humbled quickly. Every week is a new challenge.

"We all know that as a team, but we just have to focus on getting better day-by-day and honing in on the small details. I think that's what's going to separate us. It's still early in the year. Going into our second game, we know what we need to correct. Like I said before, every week's a new challenge. You have to bring the intensity no matter what."

If used properly, being served some humble pie can be a good thing.

"I think the biggest thing is learning from our mistakes from what we saw on film," Broncos receiver Courtland Sutton said to the media on Thursday. "There were things that we did well, things that we didn't do well. Being able to build on what we did well, make that last longer throughout the game, and minimize our mistakes. I would say one of the things I've seen from the team over the past few days, since the game, is an attitude of accountability, an attitude of wanting to get better and improving so that we can maximize these days leading up into Jacksonville."

Teams face adversity; it's a matter of how they respond. Denver gets its first test on Sunday.

What can certainly help the Broncos is playing at home.

"A big spark," Nix said when asked about the spark Broncos Country could provide. "There's nothing like a home-field advantage, nothing like playing at home. I know, as an away team, what it's like to go and play in a loud environment. It's definitely not easy. There are a lot of variables and things that go into it, a lot of communication tactics. It's just not easy, and that's what the crowd does. The crowd makes it not easy for them.

"So hopefully we'll have, like we always do, a sellout, hopefully we'll have a loud environment, and I expect it to be a really fun time being the home opener. I expect it to be loud. Essentially, what it is, it's a playoff game. So I expect it to be that kind of environment, sort of like we had at the end of the season last year."

title: Congress Is Trying to Rip Away College Athletes’ Hard-Earned Money
description: The Protect College Sports Act will only protect the NCAA’s billions. It deserves to go down in flames.
fullText:
If you watched the first week of college football last weekend, you saw a well-funded campaign to pass the Protect College Sports Act, or PCSA. College GameDay, ESPN's flagship pregame show, hosted Texas Senator Ted Cruz to build support for the legislation. He was largely booed throughout his appearance. Cruz was interviewed by former Indianapolis Colts punter Pat McAfee, who echoed the bill's supporters by saying that college sports were in "absolute chaos," suggesting that Congress needed to act.

Perhaps the most visible proponent of the bill is Nick Saban, who was the head football coach at the University of Alabama for most of this century. He now works as an analyst on ESPN. Saban has testified before Congress to support the bill and filmed a $10 million ad campaign with Deion Sanders, the Hall of Fame NFL player who now coaches at the University of Colorado.

"The Protect College Sports Act ends the NIL chaos in college athletics by protecting our student-athletes and teams and safeguarding women's sports and Olympic programs," he tells viewers in one version of the ad. "Join the winning team today and help protect this American tradition."

What Saban declined to mention is that the bill would "protect college sports" from the athletes who play them. The PCSA is a life raft for the NCAA, its conferences, and its schools after illegally suppressing college athletes' earning potential for decades. College athletes were finally able to pursue fair-market compensation for their services over the last few years thanks to a series of major court rulings. Now the NCAA and its allies are trying to turn back the clock to keep as much of the money that college athletes generate as possible.

The bill, like any major legislation in Congress, is the product of a thousand smaller compromises between different factions of lawmakers. There are more than a few things in the PSCA that would appeal to many college sports fans. A variety of restrictions on coaching hires and recruitment would likely appeal to those alienateed by last year's Lane Kiffen-to-LSU extravaganza, though the bill does not cap compensation for coaches or administrators. Every good thing in the PSCA is a sweetener designed to make its real purpose easier to swallow.

The PSCA's centerpiece is a harsh earnings cap for all college athletes. At minimum, those athletes could collectively receive only 22 percent of the revenue derived from their performances through their schools and conferences. There are a variety of conditions that could raise that cap for individual schools to accommodate women's sports and Olympic events, but not by much and not for everyone. This would effectively entrench a recent court settlement—more on that later—into federal law for ten years unless Congress reauthorizes it. The NFL, NHL, and NBA distribute between 45 and 50 percent of their revenue to players by comparison.

The bill also sharply limits athletes' ability to switch schools by only allowing it to happen once without penalty. Future transfers would cost athletes a year of eligibility, which would be capped at five years, outside of a few narrow exceptions—if their school eliminates a sport, for example, or a head coach is fired or hired elsewhere. To further reduce athletes' bargaining power, the PSCA would impose a strict recruiting window of between two to five weeks. This would constrain athletes' ability to shop around for the best deal, so to speak, after proving themselves.

In addition to all of this, the NCAA and its components would receive two long-sought objectives. One is preemption of state laws. By legislating on these issues, Congress would be explicitly barring state legislatures from passing their own laws to regulate compensation and other key issues for college athletes. Second, and even more importantly, the PSCA gives the NCAA immunity from federal antitrust laws when it enforces rules on compensation, transfers, broadcast rights, and more among member schools and conferences. Federal antitrust laws have been a powerful tool for college athletes to keep at least some of the wealth that they generate for themselves. With the PSCA, Congress would slam that door shut.

Arrayed against the bill are labor and civil-rights groups that have strongly criticized the PSCA for what it changes and what it preserves. In a letter to lawmakers last month, the AFL-CIO warned that the proposed law would be a major step backward for college athletes' rights. "The bill empowers the NCAA to unilaterally set rules for athletes, shielded from antitrust liability, with no suggestion that the rules ever be collectively bargained with athletes at the table," the labor organization argued.

The NAACP also criticized the bill and urged lawmakers to vote against it, arguing that it would be harmful to Black students who make up a majority of players on the most lucrative college sports. "You have coaches that have been doing this for decades now, and unfortunately, the players did not have the same rights," Derrick Johnson, the organization's president, said in an interview on ESPN earlier this week. "Now that players have rights, they're saying it's unstable. I watched college football this weekend. Every stand of every game I watched was full. People were excited. The game is as rich as it has ever been. TV revenue is up."

The bill's greatest compromise is an explicit neutrality on whether college athletes are employees or non-employees. "This title is neutral on, and does nothing to alter, employee or non-employee status for student athletes," the bill's proposed text reads. Federal laws can be vague or silent on certain matters, but I'm struggling to think of another example where Congress explicitly declined to reach a decision like this in black-letter law.

"What this bill does at its core is to protect a system of exploitation," Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy said earlier this week at an event with the PCSA's opponents. "This bill protects the billions of dollars that coaches and sports industry executives are making over the suppression of compensation for some of the most highly valued athletes in the world. This bill seeks to give an unprecedented antitrust exemption to an industry that is violating the law every single day."

Not every college team or sport is profitable, but college sports as a whole is a multi-billion dollar industry. ESPN, for example, paid $5.64 billion for a twelve-year deal to broadcast the College Football Playoffs in 2012 when they were first introduced. Two years ago, the network signed an extension with the NCAA and its components to broadcast the games through 2031 for $7.8 billion. This is just the playoffs, with the Big 10 and the SEC also reaching multi-billion agreements with the major broadcast networks for regular-season games. And it's not just college football: Networks now pay $1 billion a year to air the annual men's basketball March Madness tournament. Some of those networks' parent companies have lobbied, both officially and unofficially, on the bill's behalf in recent weeks.

Until recently, none of that money went to college athletes. The NCAA long championed the idea that its student-athletes should not be paid or compensated to preserve amateurism in college sports. NCAA rules allowed it to punish players, coaches, and schools who offered any sort of financial benefits to players beyond a limited number of scholarships. To that end, the association also opposed any efforts to classify players as employees, to allow them to unionize, or to accept any brand-endorsement deals from third parties.

Major American sports leagues are generally structured as cartels, where member teams work together to set costs and restrict worker employment and compensation. Federal antitrust law does not look kindly upon this sort of arrangement. If businesses in most other industries colluded to raise prices for consumers, depress employees' wages, or prevent workers from changing jobs, they would be engaging in illegal anti-competitive practices that could open them up to major legal consequences.

Every major American sports league has two features that prevent this: a collective-bargaining agreement with athletes that maintains labor peace, and an antitrust exemption that shields the league from litigation over anticompetitive practices. Major League Baseball has a judicially created exemption to antitrust laws thanks to a 1924 Supreme Court ruling. Other major leagues have partial exemptions to antitrust laws by act of Congress.

The Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961, for example, allows the NFL and its teams to collectively negotiate broadcast-rights packages with the networks. In exchange for this exemption, the law also prohibits the NFL from broadcasting games on Friday and Saturday for most of the season to preserve interest in high school and college football on those respective days.

To secure congressional approval of the AFL-NFL merger in 1966, the NFL also agreed to create expansion teams in certain markets favored by key lawmakers. Two key members of congressional leadership at the time, Representative Hale Boggs and Senator Russell Long, pressured then-Commissioner Pete Rozelle to promise an expansion team in their state by threatening to kill the antitrust exemption bill required for the merger. Rozelle agreed to their terms, and the New Orleans Saints began operations that same year.

Congress, when it wants to do so, can use the promise of antitrust immunity to extract meaningful changes and reforms from sports leagues. This time, the NCAA is hoping to get everything it wants without giving up anything it wouldn't be losing anyway. It is implacably opposed to recognizing college athletes as workers, fearing that they would be obligated to the provide them with the basic workplace rights that every American receives, and it does not have a statutory or judicial exemption to federal antitrust laws, despite its past occasional claims to the contrary.

As a result, the NCAA faced a wave of federal lawsuits over player compensation over the past decade. The first and most momentous ruling came in NCAA v. O'Bannon in 2014 when Judge Claudia Wilken, a federal judge in California, ruled that the association's rules forbidding athletes from profiting from "name, image, and likeness" deals, or NIL deals, violated federal antitrust law. After O'Bannon, other groups of college athletes filed a lawsuit to challenge the NCAA's restrictions on education-related compensation.

Those cases were also consolidated under Wilken, who partially ruled in favor of the athletes. In 2021, the Supreme Court unanimously upheld her injunction against the NCAA over its restrictions. The case, NCAA v. Alston, went about as badly as it could have gone for the association. Justices from across the ideological spectrum excoriated its antitrust claims. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, raising concerns about "exploiting" college athletes, warned in a concurring opinion that other NCAA rules might face a similar fate.

Finally, in NCAA v. House, the association reached a settlement with former and then-current athletes to end multiple antitrust lawsuits, which Wilken approved last year. Among the settlement's terms was a $2.8 billion compensation fund for back payments for college athletes. It also allowed schools to pay their athletes directly for the first time, with a starting cap of around $20.5 million for each school. (Athletes had already won the right in court to accept NIL payments from third parties, including school boosters.) That cap is scheduled to last for a decade with periodic increases after each school year. The settlement forms the starting point for the PSCA, though Congress has gone well beyond it to unfairly constrain college athletes' earning and bargaining power.

Perhaps the most galling aspect of the PSCA lobbying blitz is the face of it. Nick Saban is undoubtedly the best college football head coach of the past quarter century. He was also handsomely compensated for it. The University of Alabama paid him between $3.5 and $11 million each year between 2007 and 2023. Saban was paid a fair-market value for his labor, and he was able to leverage his success into greater earnings along the way. The players he led and coached had no such opportunities while playing for him.

Even as the NCAA fought to prevent college athletes at Alabama and other schools from pursuing NIL deals, Saban was able to pursue them himself. He signed an endorsement deal with insurance giant Aflac in August 2019 that made him one of the faces of its complex advertising strategy. Had one of his players signed that same deal that year, they would have lost their eligibility to participate in NCAA sports.

Fortunately, this legislation might be one victory that even Saban can't achieve. The good news is that the PSCA might not become law in the 119th Congress. While the Senate is on course to pass its version of the bill later this month, the House adjourned on Wednesday until after the November midterm elections. Speaker Mike Johnson's decision left a host of other major legislative issues on ice until the lame-duck session this winter. If the clock runs out on the PSCA, college sports and the athletes who play them will be better off for it.

title: Mike Thibault helped build the Connecticut Sun. Now he'll be rightfully honored: Mike Anthony
description: Thibault coached the Connecticut Sun for 10 seasons, twice reaching the WNBA Finals.
fullText:
In the spring of 2003, Mike Thibault took the stage in Mohegan Sun Arena and was introduced as the first coach in Connecticut Sun history.

The Orlando Miracle had relocated to Uncasville. Thibault, 52 at the time, had never coached women's basketball. He had no staff, beyond the few front-office folks who hired him. He hadn't met a single player. If he didn't have doubts about his new basketball world, he sure was anxious.

"I remember having my press conference and, later that night, sitting in the arena by myself," Thibault said. "I sat there and thought to myself, 'What the hell have I just done?"

Thibault, a longtime NBA scout and assistant coach, made a leap of faith, not knowing at the time he had also made a massive jump toward shaping a career that should land him in the Naismith Hall of Fame.

Coaching the Sun, the first WNBA team without the backing of an NBA franchise, positioned Thibault to eventually become the winningest coach in league history. And on Sunday, all these years later, as the Sun come down the stretch of their 24th and final season, Thibault will sit in a full arena to be honored, appropriately so. He will be honored as a Sun 'Legend' following a 1 p.m. game against the Minnesota Lynx.

"It will be fun to go back," Thibault said this week, shortly after returning from Germany, where he coached the Belgian national team in the World Cup. "It's always a little bittersweet because I have good memories, but the ending wasn't the way I would have liked to have it go."

Coach-franchise basketball marriages rarely end without contentious vibes. Thibault led the Sun for 10 years - with eight winning seasons and trips to the WNBA Finals in 2004 and 2005 - but was fired after a conference finals loss to Indiana in 2012, when the Sun finished 25-9 as the Eastern Conference's No. 1 seed.

The franchise in 2010 had committed to a rebuild, which involved trading Lindsay Whalen and the No. 2 draft pick to Minnesota for Renee Montgomery and the No. 1 pick, which became Tina Charles. Two years later, the Sun, even faster than initial expectations, were really good again. The franchise thought Thibault should have delivered a championship.

With a victory over the Sun in the Finals.

"I tried to downplay it," Thibault said. "You don't want to put pressure on players, that they have to 'Do it for Coach.' It had to be about them, and it was. But I probably, silently, when I left, put a curse on Connecticut in my mind, that I'm going to win one first."

Each party, ultimately, wound up just fine after the parting. The Sun, after a few down years, gained traction and made two more Finals appearances under Curt Miller. Thibault, meanwhile, coached the Mystics for 10 seasons. His 20-year record in the WNBA was 379-289. He was passed in July for the all-time victories record by Cheryl Reeve, Minnesota Lynx coach since 2010.

So the bullet points of his resume are as follows: A California native, Thibault worked with the Showtime Lakers and Michael Jordan's Bulls in the 1980s. He was a head coach in the World Basketball League (Calgary 88's) and the Continental Basketball Association (Omaha Racers) before returning to the NBA as an assistant coach with the Bucks in 1998-2002. Then he became one of the most successful coaches in WNBA's first quarter-century.

Thibault and wife Nanci wound up raising a family - which became a prominent basketball family - in Connecticut because of the opportunity to coach the Sun.

"As an NBA person, I was always going to be an assistant coach," Thibault said. "I wasn't going to be a head coach unless you're in one of those situations where you're an assistant and the head coach gets fired and you take over. That didn't seem the way to go about things. I was intrigued by being a head coach. I was intrigued by coaching the women's game. My daughter had just started playing, and that was a family discussion.

"I had friends who coached in the W and said if I tried it I would like it. I thought, 'OK, I'll try it, and if I don't like it I'll go back to the NBA.' We fell in love with it. While I was in Connecticut alone, I had a couple offers to go back to the NBA and we said, 'Why we would do that? We like what we're doing. We like the people we're working with.' And the side thing we had never even thought about, because we played in the summer, I actually got to see my kids more, all their sporting events or music, whatever it was. And then in the summer, they made themselves a part of what we did. Our family was happy, so it worked."

Carly Thibault-DuDonis is entering her fifth year as the head coach of the Fairfield women's basketball team. Eric Thibault, a long-time staff member under his father, primarily in Washington, took over as head coach of the Mystics when Mike stepped down in 2022. Eric is currently an assistant with the Lynx, under Reeve, so Sunday is a homecoming for him, too. Thibault-DuDonis will attend the game. Both coaches began their basketball pursuits by shooting hoops and chasing around Sun players at Mohegan Sun Arena.

The early years were fresh and fun. Rebecca Lobo played her final professional season with the team. Nykesha Sales, beloved here for her Bloomfield and UConn roots, was the best player. The team lost the 2004 Finals to Seattle and returned a year later, losing to Sacramento with Lindsay Whalen injured and hobbling.

The Sun will relocate to Houston after this season as a successful franchise, no doubt – but without ever winning a championship. Still, Thibault's 10 years created something the Connecticut basketball community, and the WNBA, should be proud of.

"I've been impressed with how the Sun have handled this last season," Thibault said. "I think they've been classy about it all the way around. I feel sad that they're moving. I get the business reasons. It's tough. The big markets are mostly going to win out. But I'm also proud that we were the first non-NBA organization to make it work. The stuff we did to get it started, from ownership on down and the Tribe and everyone involved. It was a good group to be around."

The Thibault family lived in East Lyme during their time in Connecticut. Mike and Nanci now live in Alexandria, Va., just outside of D.C. Thibault, 75, was hired as Belgian coach in January 2025, a role he is expected to continue through the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. Already, he has coached in two Olympics, as an assistant on Team USA under Anne Donovan in 2008 and Reeve in 2024.

"It's amazing that an orange, round ball has afforded us - my family and me - the life we've had, the people we've met, the places we've gone," Thibault said.

Thibault has touched just about every level of basketball, on both the men's and women's sides. The Hall of Fame hasn't called yet. It really should. His resume is worthy. It took shape here in Connecticut. He helped the Sun, and the Sun helped him. It was the perfect partnership to get something started. It's certainly worth honoring as the Sun retrace their history and wave goodbye to our state.

The 25-year-old winger joined Barça from Newcastle United in the summer for a fee of €70 million plus €10 million in add-ons.

Tuchel & co. will play Spain in their first game, meaning Gordon will come up against some of his club teammates, including Pedri and Rodri. Following that, England will take on Czechia (twice) and Croatia.

title: Chinese companies doubled down on science after US tech restrictions
description: Affected Chinese companies adjusted their sources of knowledge to stay competitive.
fullText:
Chinese firms that were restricted from accessing specific technologies created in the United States increased their use of science publications to boost innovation, according to an analysis of patent citations and scientific publications1 in Science today.

Researchers examined how Chinese firms adjusted their ways of accessing knowledge after the US government put them on an Entity List. The list prevents those on it from licensing certain materials and engaging with joint research and development projects. The US government says that the Entity List is designed to safeguard national security: It began putting large Chinese firms on the list in 2018 when the China–US geopolitical relationship became tense.

After their inclusion on the list, Chinese firms produced more patents that cited scientific publications than did companies similar to them that had not been sanctioned. They also published more scientific articles than did unsanctioned companies, the article says.

The finding is notable because it shows the “unintended consequences” of US export controls, says Cong Cao, a researcher of innovation policy at the University of Nottingham Ningbo China.

“Whether or not one supports technology controls, it is important to recognize that they can come with costs,” adds Dinsha Mistree, a political economist at Stanford University in California.

Although Chinese firms boosted their engagement with science after restrictions were introduced, Kenneth Huang, a researcher of innovation and technology management at the National University of Singapore, says the authors cannot be sure that a Chinese firm being placed on the Entity List actually caused this shift or whether other factors were at play.

Other studies have assessed the impact of US sanctions on Chinese innovation. But the latest analysis “uses some of the best data, as well as rigorous methods for such an analysis”, says Mistree.

To show the effect of US sanctions on Chinese innovation, the authors of the latest analysis used data sets spanning 2010–22 from several sources, including the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA) — which is China’s patent and trademark office — the article-indexing platform Web of Science and the China Stock Market and Accounting Research Database.

The researchers began by identifying long-term trends: they found that Chinese companies in general, whether sanctioned or not, deepened their engagement with the scientific community during the studied period. For example, the number of patents granted by CNIPA that cited at least one scientific paper increased more than 18-fold, from 5,225 in 2010 to 94,441 in 2022. Patents granted to Chinese firms by the US Patent and Trade Office jumped more than 13-fold, from 452 to 6,071. However, US inventors and firms still lead the world in the use of scientific knowledge in patents.

The authors then compared Chinese companies that were included on the US Entity List between 2010 and 2022with those that were not over the same period. To ensure the comparison was robust, they compared sanctioned firms with non-sanctioned firms that shared similar characteristics, such as their industry, owners and location.

The authors shows that Chinese firms subject to sanctions produced 72.3% more patents that cite at least one scientific publication than did similar non-sanctioned companies. Sanctioned companies also published 33.3% more papers indexed in the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, China's largest academic database of papers, than did their non-sanctioned peers. In Web of Science, they published 85.2% more.

Mistree says that he would expect Chinese firms to increase their publications and the number of patents that cite papers, irrespective of whether they were sanctioned, owing to China's substantial investments in science and technology during this time. “What the authors show so convincingly is that the Chinese companies that were subject to US sanctions pursued an even more intensive science and technology approach than they would have otherwise. These Chinese companies seem to double down on innovation when they are sanctioned,” he adds.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-02946-y

Wang, J., Li, X. & Wang, Y. Science 393, 1196–1199 (2026).
